There's a reason the Daruma Temple is my favorite temple in all of Japan. 🇯🇵 And one of the key experiences of my Japan Leadership Experience.

I fell in love with darumas over a decade ago when I was living in Japan, and the figure has become my "mascot" in many ways!

The daruma doll embodies the proverb: "fall down seven times, get up eight."

When you have a goal, you fill in the doll's left eye. 

It serves as a visual reminder of the path of learning toward success. And when you achieve your goal, you fill in the other eye!

People bring their darumas here when their goal is complete, to be burned at the end of the year, a ritual of persistence, reflection, and renewal.

On this most recent visit, I brought a participant's daruma back to the temple from a past Japan Leadership Experience, at his request, for his completed goal of finishing his master's degree! (Congrats again Glenn Wilson!)

We don't just visit the temple. We take part in a Zen meditation with the head priest and talk about what these traditions teach us about business and leadership.

This is what makes my Japan Leadership Experience more than a trip: culture, reflection, and connection, alongside a remarkable group of global leaders. 

Plus special insights, curated experiences, and personal connections that I've developed over eleven years of living and working in Japan.

Going to the GEMBA makes people feel that they are important

Learning to LEAD, Leading to LEARN by Katie Anderson is full of leadership gems, so simple but yet so powerful.
The book follows the learnings of a key TOYOTA manager, Isao Yoshino, captured by Katie through a series of conversations.

Katie and Isao Yoshino layout the principle that going to the gemba, “you demonstrate that you care about them”. The act of going to the gemba allows you to enter their world is a respectful & humble way, seeing what they experience everyday.

In reflecting on this, isn't that the real reason the method was developed, to build a connection between Senior Leaders and front line team members? Who would typically only meet in the worst of circumstances. 

I recall years ago, the presence of a Senior Leader on the Shop Floor created so much fear and apprehension. This occurrence was so rare, that everyone was fearful and found ways to avoid being around the Leader. This can never be the environment we want to create. A Senior Leader needs to humble themselves and visit the gemba,


Thanks Katie Anderson, for valuable insights from deep within TOYOTA, plus a really enjoyable read.

𝗗𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 

Vor rund 70 Jahren hat ein einfacher Stahlbehälter effiziente und globale Logistik und Supply Chain möglich gemacht. 

Ich bin überzeugt: GenAI ist für die Supply Chain der nächste Container-Moment.

Wir wechseln gerade von Chatbots zu agentischer KI. Das sind Systeme, die eigenständig Daten sammeln, Angebot und Nachfrage abgleichen und koordinieren. SCM-Systeme wie APS, OMS, TMS, WMS, Visibility-Tools,  etc, die bisher nebeneinander standen, fangen endlich an, miteinander zu sprechen.
Und die Planerinnen und Planer? Ihre Rolle wird anspruchsvoller. Wenn die KI die Routine übernimmt, bleibt die eigentlich schwierige Arbeit: erkennen, wann das System danebenliegt. Das braucht mehr kritisches Denken, nicht weniger.
Genau darüber habe ich im #LogTech Podcast mit Steffen Liermann und Jannik Nonnenkamp  gesprochen. Es ging um agentische KI als Übersetzer zwischen Mensch und Algorithmus, um digitale Zwillinge im Onboarding und darum, was hybride Mensch-KI-Teams für HR bedeuten. 

Kurzer Spoiler für alle, die sich fragen, ob man nicht erst die Stammdaten bereinigen sollte: Der Container hat damals niemanden gefragt, ob die Häfen bereit waren.

Die Diskussion hat viel Spaß gemacht - hoffe, euch gefällt die Folge.

𝗚𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆'𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝟬.𝟮 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗚𝗗𝗣. 𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗮'𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝟮𝟯 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁. 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆.

Daniel Stelter and Jan Mischke discussed McKinsey Global Institute's new study, 𝗖𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 on the bto podcast. Very clear insight, Germany is now nearly the most expensive location in almost every industry the study examined (semiconductors, chemicals, batteries, pharma). The cost gap ranges from 40% to over 250%, depending on the sector.

The root causes are not mysterious. 
🎷 𝗪𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 are three to five times higher than in China, without matching productivity. 
🎷 A 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝘁 takes 200 days in Germany — versus 60 in the US and 40 in China. 
🎷 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 on the Rhine runs above $150 per megawatt-hour.

The study provides four concrete levers to improve: 
🎷 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 through 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿, 𝗽𝗿𝗲-𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 
🎷 let 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗿𝗯 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗴𝗮𝗽
🎷 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁  
🎷 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, industrial AI, solid-state batteries, semiconductor equipment, rather than on cost alone. 

One more number I found interesting: Jan mentioned (from an earlier study) that Germany currently loses roughly 1 percentage point of productivity growth annually due to insufficient market clearing — i.e., legacy structures and rigid labor rules that keep capital and people locked into underperforming firms for too long. This is remarkable. Daniel advocated for the Danish 𝗙𝗹𝗲𝘅𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 model 

McKinsey estimates 30 to 80 percent of the gap is closable this way. Waiting is the most expensive option.

Super interesting interview and report (link in the comments).

A personal experiment in AI-assisted supply chain planning

A few weeks ago I showed a colleague a demo of a supply chain planning application I had built. A sharp, experienced supply chain planner who has been navigating demand forecasting, capacity management, and supplier risk for over a decade. She is exactly the kind of person who should be excited about AI.

“That’s cool,” she said politely when I opened the app. Then I clicked through the tabs, demand forecasting with manual overrides and natural language input, capacity planning by resource and plant, a bottleneck analysis with cost scenarios, a bill-of-materials navigator, an executive S&OP summary with assessment of 3 capacity scenarios, a supplier risk map, and more. 
Her tone changed: “Wait. Did you build this yourself?” When I told her it took about 30 hours, she went quiet for a moment. Then: “I had absolutely no idea this was possible.”

That reaction — the quiet before the questions — is something I have now seen several times. In boardrooms, in workshops, in informal conversations with supply chain professionals at every level. And the discussions that follow are always similar
🎷 “But how? I thought you needed a whole development team for something like this.”
🎷 “We’ve been using ChatGPT for writing emails. This is... completely different.”
🎷 “Do we still need that APS implementation we’ve been scoping for the last 6 months?”
🎷 “Can I show this to our Head of Supply Chain? To our COO? Today?”

The gap between what most people believe AI can do today and what it actually can do is enormous. I am not talking about theoretical futures or research papers. I am talking about right now. A planner with deep domain knowledge can build functional business applications in days, not months. I have to say: this genuinely blew my mind.

Here are some screenshots of the app on demand planning (including natural language input to change the statistical forecast), BOM navigator, exec S&OP overview of scenarios, gap to budget etc and a supplier risk map & flows.

“𝗪𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀 — 𝘀𝗶𝘅𝘁𝘆 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗮𝗽 𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.”

And then the data teams sat down together for the first time and compared the ERP systems.

The same standard bolt appeared as MRB5-SS-HEX in one system and SLT-8-20-INOX in the other, with two further variants across two additional databases. Identical components, incompatible naming conventions, 60.000 parts multiplied across four systems, and a saving that was perfectly real but completely invisible to anyone trying to read across them. An opportunity impossible to see.

The traditional answer was an IT project. Three years, a budget of 2 Mio EUR, a waterfall plan with phases and milestones and a go-live date that kept moving because the problem was harder than the architecture diagram had suggested. By the time the data was finally clean and the components were properly matched, the savings window had closed. Competitors had already moved, the relevant suppliers had been contracted elsewhere, and the people who had championed the initiative had mostly moved on to other roles. By the time the data was clean, nobody cared about the savings anymore.

This is the trap that 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁-𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 walks into with remarkable consistency, not because the opportunity is wrong, but because the time it takes to see it clearly always seems to exceed the time the market gives you to act on it. The saving was never the question. The question was always whether anyone could find it fast enough to matter.

Kai Hoberg and I are working on something to help organizations find what is already sitting in their data, faster than a traditional IT project can move. More before summer.

𝗜 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺, 𝘄𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 - 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗱. (𝗖𝗙𝗢)

How does a company free up 8 Mio EUR in working capital and lose 96 Mio EUR in the same year?

The answer usually starts with a slide that looked completely convincing. A 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀 showing inventory levels sitting well above the best-in-class range, a clear gap against what the top performers in the industry were holding, and a straightforward recommendation to bring the numbers in line. Finance approved it, the board noted it as a sign of improving capital discipline, and the Q3 balance sheet looked better than it had in years. 8 Mio EUR freed, a compelling story ready for the next investor update.

Then a port strike hit, a critical supplier ran 3 weeks late, and what followed was the kind of variability that shows up every 18 months or so, which the organization had always managed without much drama. Except this time, the buffer was gone, the stock had been cut to benchmark levels, and 2 customers who needed the product went out of stock and moved to a competitor. Revenue lost: 96 Mio EUR. The write-off was twelve times the original saving.

The benchmark had done exactly what benchmarks do: it told the team what their peers were holding. What it did not say was what that inventory was actually doing, which customer commitments it was protecting, which supply risks it was quietly absorbing, which revenue it was underwriting in the background. That information was never in the slide because nobody had thought to put it there, and nobody senior had thought to ask.

In theory, aligning with best-in-class inventory ratios improves capital efficiency. In practice, resilience is invisible until it disappears, and by then the cost of finding out what it was worth tends to hit all at once.

Kai Hoberg and I are building something to help finance and operations teams ask the right questions before the cut, not after the crisis. More before summer.

It is one of the most common questions heard in a boardroom after a supply chain crisis, and it is almost always asked by someone who, three months earlier, was sitting in a quarterly review that ended with the words "operations are running smoothly." The revenue was up, the new market entry was ahead of plan, and nobody had mentioned  Supply Chain because nobody needed to. When it works, it is invisible, and invisibility in that room feels like the highest possible endorsement a supply chain team will ever receive.

Then a single component goes on allocation somewhere in an overseas supplier network, and within days, the picture looks completely different. Shipments stop, customers escalate, and the CEO who was closing slides with quiet confidence is now standing in front of a crisis that seems to have appeared from nowhere. Except it did not appear from nowhere. The risk was visible in reports that nobody had read, in risk registers that nobody had requested, in the heads of planners who had flagged it quietly and moved on because nobody senior had ever thought to ask.

The answer to "why did we not see this coming?" is almost always the same: because Supply Chain was not in the room when it mattered. Not because the information was missing, but because the function had no standing invitation to the conversations where the real decisions were being made. It was managed from a distance, measured on cost, and noticed only when something broke.
The companies that navigate disruptions best are not always the ones with the most sophisticated risk models. They are the ones where leadership understood, before any crisis arrived, that Supply Chain is the architecture of the business, not a support function whose importance is discovered only in a post-mortem.

[Mini Interview] Planning the Unplannable: SCM, McKinsey, and the AI Revolution
 
Meet Knut Alicke, he is a Supply Chain Therapist with 30 years experience in improving supply chain performance (icon-scm, McKinsey). He build and led the Supply Chain Practice at McKinsey and is actively teaching as a Professor at the University of Cologne, Karlsruhe and SKEMA. 
 
Tell us your journey with SCM and McKinsey? 
 
I got into Supply Chain during my time at the IFL, KIT Karlsruhe - working on my PhD and Habilitation I joined a spin-off (icon-scm) of the Institute working on a planning solution for Hewlett Packard.
 
It was in the late 90’ies, HP did grow volume and complexity like crazy and they were looking for a planning system.
 
Very cool experience of smart business people and us beeing able to create software very fast.
 
Looking back a lot of companies do not have the maturity today that we created 25 years ago.  
 
In 2004 I was approached by McKinsey, joined, build and led their SC Practice for 21 years and now working on a mix of helping startups, teaching, still being active as a Senior Advisor for McKinsey. 
 
 
Tell us about your book Source To Sold?
 
Radu (my co-author) and joked about the lack of Supply Chain talent in the C-Suite. And we decided to work on it - started the first Interview and got more into it, more interviews (26 in total), developed a framework (the CHAIN framework).
 
The book is a collection of individual stories of leaders who spend a significant part of their professional live in SC.
 
It is about the similarities - described in the CHAIN framework - Collaborative, Holistic, Agile, Influential and Narrative are the common elements. 
 
A great read for everyone in Supply Chain. 
 
 
Tell us about your vision of GenAi and Planning in SCM?
 
GenAI / Agentic AI will change the way we operate Supply Chains - similar to the disruption the container had on global supply chains. The challenge in todays supply chains is the lack of experience in the planning systems.
 
They assume a perfect world and are surprised when things go wrong (a delay of a supplier, lower capacity of a production line, etc).
 
This is where the „human“ planner comes in - with years of experience, to fix the plan. GenAI will help to bridge the gap, I call this the experiential ontology. GenAI will sit between the planner and the APS/ERP layer and finally create and execute realistic plans. 
 
Another very powerful area is CI - like a gemba walk in manufacturing - we will see specilized Supply Chain Avatars helping to solve behavioral problems.
 
As an example, the overforecast of sales is not because sales has no clue, but because of bad experience (allocation etc) and thus the only way sales can get more deliveries.
 
Local incentives and decision making is the main blocker for proper decision making in the E2E Supply Chain. A CI bot (aka SC Avatar) will help to bridge by „coaching“ Sales and Supply Chains on how to improve the collaboration.

🎷 𝐀 𝐦𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤 𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭. Critical tacit knowledge lives in veteran planners’ heads and is at risk of disappearing as that workforce retires.
🎷 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐀𝐈 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥. By interacting conversationally with planners and capturing decision reasoning, GenAI can build a compounding “experiential ontology” that improves decisions over time.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮 €𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝗖𝗠 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗲𝗱.

The IT project had taken two years and significant organizational energy. The new integrated planning platform was state of the art, with constraint-based optimization, AI-driven demand sensing, and real-time inventory visibility across the network. The implementation team had done everything the vendor prescribed.

Go-live was in March. By June, the planners were back on spreadsheets. The system had been designed around process templates that assumed a supply chain the company didn’t have. 
🎷 The master data was inconsistent. 
🎷 The demand signal inputs didn’t reflect how customers actually ordered. 
🎷 The optimization engine was solving for a cost structure that hadn’t been updated in three years.

Technology implementation and supply chain understanding are not the same thing. An ERP or planning tool is only as good as the logic it encodes. And that logic requires someone who understands demand variability, lead time dynamics, inventory trade-offs, and the network structure deeply enough to translate operational reality into system parameters.

The gap between what planning systems model and what planners actually know is one of the most underestimated problems in supply chain. Most implementations treat it as a data problem. It is, in fact, a knowledge problem,  one that no software vendor can solve on your behalf.

The €12 million question was not “which system?” It was “does our organization understand the supply chain well enough to use it?” That question should always come first.

A personal experiment in AI-assisted supply chain planning

A few weeks ago I showed a colleague a demo of a supply chain planning application I had built. A sharp, experienced supply chain planner who has been navigating demand forecasting, capacity management, and supplier risk for over a decade. She is exactly the kind of person who should be excited about AI.

“That’s cool,” she said politely when I opened the app. Then I clicked through the tabs, demand forecasting with manual overrides and natural language input, capacity planning by resource and plant, a bottleneck analysis with cost scenarios, a bill-of-materials navigator, an executive S&OP summary with assessment of 3 capacity scenarios, a supplier risk map, and more. 
Her tone changed: “Wait. Did you build this yourself?” When I told her it took about 30 hours, she went quiet for a moment. Then: “I had absolutely no idea this was possible.”

That reaction — the quiet before the questions — is something I have now seen several times. In boardrooms, in workshops, in informal conversations with supply chain professionals at every level. And the discussions that follow are always similar
🎷 “But how? I thought you needed a whole development team for something like this.”
🎷 “We’ve been using ChatGPT for writing emails. This is... completely different.”
🎷 “Do we still need that APS implementation we’ve been scoping for the last 6 months?”
🎷 “Can I show this to our Head of Supply Chain? To our COO? Today?”

The gap between what most people believe AI can do today and what it actually can do is enormous. I am not talking about theoretical futures or research papers. I am talking about right now. A planner with deep domain knowledge can build functional business applications in days, not months. I have to say: this genuinely blew my mind.

Here are some screenshots of the app on demand planning (including natural language input to change the statistical forecast), BOM navigator, exec S&OP overview of scenarios, gap to budget etc and a supplier risk map & flows. 

More details on what I did, how I built the test company and the S&OP app in a longer article in the comments. 

I'm very happy to share the test company I built for your own experiements - just let me know in the comments or DM me. 

Amazing times ahead.

#FelgendreherAndFriends masterclass is back - very happy to talk about my favorite topic of #RiskAndResilience with Boris Felgendreher and Nico Nuerbchen. We had a great discussion, insights and covered a lot. 

Every company says it learned from the lockdown during the pandemic. Then the next shock arrives, the task force reconvenes, and everyone starts from zero again.

We keep calling these events #blackswans, unpredictable events with massive and disruptive impact. But to be honest, most of them are #greyrhinos, huge impact, but somehow predictable. 
🎷 The Strait of Hormuz was not a surprise. 
🎷 Chip concentration was not a surprise. 
🎷 Rare earth dependency was not a surprise. 
We simply did not act on what we could already see. And "the route is open again" is not the same as back to normal. The backlog outlives the headline by months.

In MedTech as Nico pointed out the stakes are high, a stockout is not lost margin but patients at risk.

Two important things to remember: 
➡️ First, the three numbers Ilse Henne of thyssenkrupp puts on the table: Days of Awareness, Days of Survival, Days of Recovery. Most companies cannot answer the first one.
➡️ Second, the language problem. A risk program presented as a cost request dies in the boardroom. The same program presented as revenue at risk gets funded. Resilience is a strategy and belongs to the board.

Most companies are fragile because they optimized every link until only one was left. So here is the uncomfortable one: if a Tier-3 supplier stopped shipping tomorrow, how many days would pass before you knew?

We need to promote a broader understanding. While logistics is mainly about the storage and transport of goods, SCM in a company reaches much further. It is cross-functional, end-to-end, and shaped by many decisions across the organization.
1️⃣ Cross-functional, because sales, finance, procurement, R&D, marketing, and operations all shape supply chain outcomes.
2️⃣ End-to-end, because SCM connects suppliers, factories, inventories, distribution networks, customers, and information flows.
3️⃣ Driven by many decisions, because delivery performance, availability, cost, resilience, and sustainability are the result of countless choices made across the company.
 
All these people involved manage the supply chain. That is why some SCM microfoundations deserve to be understood by everyone.

Thoughts on the future of Supply Chain, driving forces and scenarios to manage 
 
The last three decades were built on one logic: 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲, 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲, 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁. That logic is being dismantled by five forces operating simultaneously: 
🎷 𝗴𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: The trade system is no longer just about tariffs,  sanctions, export controls, industrial policy, and AI access restrictions, turning network design into a geopolitical decision.
🎷 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗜: Industrial robots and agentic AI are becoming real operational tools, but we see a bottleneck in the organizations: curiosity to explore new ideas, data quality, process redesign, and the willingness to trust AI. 
🎷 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗻: Carbon pricing, shipping decarbonization mandates, and route disruptions (Hormuz,  Suez) make the cost of distance a strategic variable, not a logistics footnote. 
🎷 𝗰𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆: Three regions control 86% of the processing capacity for the materials that power electrification, AI infrastructure, and defense modernization simultaneously, and investment is not keeping up with demand
🎷 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝘁𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗰𝗶𝗿𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆: Regulation is forcing companies to design for end-of-life before they design for production. Reverse logistics networks required to comply do not yet exist at scale.

I use those forces to develop 4 possible scenarios and reflect on how the supply chain might look in 2030 and 2040:
🎷 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 & 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀 (most probable): The world splits into blocs, but automation and AI absorb the cost of that complexity
🎷 𝗚𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗻 & 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱: Carbon pricing and shipping decarbonization reshape the economics of distance before technology fully compensates. Supply chains shorten.
🎷 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗙𝗹𝗮𝘁 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱: Geopolitical tensions ease, and AI matures fast enough to make global networks smarter and cheaper than regional ones. The upside case.
🎷 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗻𝘁 & 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗱: Fragmentation deepens, automation stalls, and companies are left with brittle networks and no technology. The tail risk nobody wants to plan for, but should

Supply chain leaders need to work on 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁, not the lowest total landed cost. A network designed for minimum reconfiguration cost builds optionality from the start. Companies may find they 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝘆𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆
